facts.item: Crankshaft main journal diameter (2.7-3.3 L engines)
facts.value: 64 mm (LN Engineering table); alternatively ~60 mm (59.971-59.990 mm) per forum posts quoting the 964 shop manual, which shares the same crank family
facts.note: This is the central unresolved conflict. LN Engineering lists 64 mm for all 2.7-3.3 L engines. The tech-racingcars wiki lists 60 mm for the 1978 3.3 (with '60-55 mm' notation suggesting two sizes). Forum posts quoting a 964 shop manual give 59.97-59.99 mm. See conflicts.

facts.value: 55 mm (54.971-54.990 mm tolerance band)
facts.note: Consistent across multiple sources. The 3.2 Carrera, 3.3 Turbo and 3.6 964 share the same rod journal diameter. Paul Frere's book also gives 55 mm.

facts.value: 22 mm (21.8 mm per Frere's book)
facts.note: Rennlist gives 22 mm; Frere's book gives 21.8 mm. The 993 narrowed this to 19 mm. Aftermarket rod vendors list big-end width of 21.74 mm. All three numbers are within 0.3 mm.

facts.value: 8 (7 main bearings plus 1 nose bearing #8 at pulley end)
facts.note: The nose bearing (#8) is a smaller plain bearing supporting the crank snout at the pulley end. Part number 964.101.138.01 covers 911/964/993/996 Turbo.

facts.value: At the pulley (fan) end of the crankshaft; the protruding snout beyond the case on a 3.2 is 60 mm long
facts.note: The nose bearing journal diameter itself was not found in any source. The 60 mm figure is the snout protrusion length from one forum post about a 3.2 Carrera.

facts.value: 42CrMo4 or CK45 forged steel
facts.note: Listed for the 930 Group 3 racing car but the same alloys are standard for Porsche road cranks. The crank is fully counterweighted and forged.

facts.value: 9 bolts for the 1978-89 3.3 L Turbo (M8 x 1.25 x 80 mm hex-head bolts with wave washers)
facts.note: The earlier 3.0 Turbo (1975-77) used 6 bolts. Multiple vendors consistently list 9 bolts for the 3.3 L flywheel.

facts.value: 126 mm (non-A/C cars)
facts.note: Design911 lists 126 mm for the 1976-89 911/930 crank pulley without A/C. Cars with A/C use a different, larger pulley arrangement.

facts.value: 6 crankpins arranged in 3 pairs at 120 degrees apart; each pair carries two rods from opposed cylinders on separate but closely adjacent pins
facts.note: The page describes 'crankpins in three levels.' In a boxer six, each opposed pair has its own crankpin (not shared like a V6), so there are 6 pins total. The firing order 1-6-2-4-3-5 with 120-degree spacing means pairs are: cyl 1+4, cyl 2+5, cyl 3+6.

facts.value: Vertically split on the crankshaft axis into left and right halves, through-bolted together
facts.note: This is the standard air-cooled 911 architecture. The crankshaft and rods are installed before the halves are joined.

facts.value: 11 through-bolts, M10 x 1.5 thread
facts.note: ARP kit 204-5405 for 3.0-3.3 L engines includes 11 studs. Design911 also sells through-bolt kits in sets of 11. There are also M8 perimeter nuts around the case joint torqued to 25 Nm. One forum post about a 2.4 engine mentions 13 through-bolts, suggesting the count may vary by era.

facts.item: Crankcase material (3.0 SC / 3.2 Carrera / 3.3 Turbo era)
facts.value: Aluminum alloy, die-cast; forum sources say close to A356.0-T6; SAE papers cite Porsche using AlSi17Cu4Mg (alloy 390) for air-cooled 911 blocks
facts.note: Early 911s (1968-1977) used magnesium cases. From the Carrera 3.0 (1976) onward, Porsche switched to aluminum. The 930 Turbo uses an aluminum case. Porsche Classic now sells new magnesium cases for pre-1977 cars only.

facts.item: Crankcase deck height (crank centerline to cylinder spigot top)
facts.value: Approximately 112.5 mm
facts.note: Forum poster measured 112.4-112.5 mm from crank center to top of cylinder spigot bore. Combined with a cylinder height of ~85.3-85.5 mm gives a total piston-to-crank distance consistent with the computed 197 mm. This is for the SC/3.2 case; the 930 Turbo shares the same case dimensions.

facts.value: 105 mm (for 3.0-3.3 L engines)
facts.note: Mahle lists the 3.0-3.3 L CIS engines as using a 105 mm cylinder case register. Machine-in cylinders for larger bores require boring the register to a larger diameter.

facts.value: Aluminum alloy barrels with Nikasil (nickel-silicon carbide) bore coating
facts.note: Nikasil was standard on all 930 Turbo cylinders. The coating is extremely hard and wear-resistant.

facts.item: Cylinder barrel length (95 mm bore, 3.0 L)
facts.value: 120 mm length, 113 mm spigot diameter
facts.note: This is for the 95 mm bore 3.0 L barrel. The 97 mm bore 3.3 L barrel dimensions were not found in any source. The barrel height is likely similar or slightly different.

facts.value: Partially finned with asymmetrical fins; the turbo cylinders have smaller fins concentrated on the lower portion, with material filling the gaps between fins on the upper portion
facts.note: This differs from naturally aspirated cylinders which are fully finned around the entire circumference. Forum posts describe this as Porsche filling material into the fin gaps. Exact fin count not found.

facts.item: Head studs total count and arrangement
facts.value: 24 studs total, 4 per cylinder, M10 x 1.5 thread
facts.note: The studs screw into the crankcase halves and pass up through the cylinder fins and into the head.

facts.value: 12 upper studs: conventional steel; 12 lower (exhaust-side) studs: Dilavar (a non-magnetic low-expansion steel alloy used in Porsche racing engines since the early 1970s)
facts.note: Dilavar studs are placed on the exhaust side where thermal cycling is most severe. ARP aftermarket replacement kits use 8740 chromoly steel for all positions.

facts.value: 23 mm
facts.note: Confirmed by the Mahle application guide PDF. The earlier 3.0 Turbo (95 mm bore) used a 22 mm pin.

facts.item: Piston ring pack (3.3 L Turbo, 98 mm bore Mahle kit)
facts.value: 1.2 mm, 1.2 mm, 3.0 mm (top compression, second compression, oil control)
facts.note: From the Mahle motorsport application guide. FVD also lists the same ring dimensions: 1.2 / 1.2 / 3.0 mm for the 930 3.3 L at 98 mm.
Confirmed in the Mahle PDF for the 930 Turbo 3.3 L to 3.4 L kit. The 3.0 Turbo (Group 3) used 35.7 mm.

facts.value: Crown volume 14.2 cc, piston weight 436 g, material 4032 forged aluminum alloy
facts.note: These are from the Mahle PS98-009 kit (7.7:1 CR, 98 mm bore). The OEM 930 Turbo uses 97 mm bore with 7.0:1 CR; the Mahle kit is a performance replacement with slightly larger bore and higher CR.

facts.value: 127 mm center-to-center (some sources give 127.75 mm)
facts.note: Mahle PDF lists 127 mm for the 3.3 L 930 Turbo. The 127.75 mm figure appears in aftermarket rod listings and may represent nominal OEM length. The tech-racingcars wiki gives 127.75 mm for the Group 3 car.

facts.value: 58 mm (1978+ 3.3 L Turbo)
facts.note: Tech-racingcars lists 'big-end bearing tunnel 58 mm' for the 1978 engine, up from 56 mm on the earlier 3.0. Some aftermarket rod vendors list 58.014 mm.

facts.value: 3/8 inch (9.525 mm), 69 mm bolt length
facts.note: Listed across multiple aftermarket rod vendors. Standard WMC bolts have 220 ksi UTS; upgraded Carrillo bolts reach 285 ksi.

facts.value: 240 mm clutch disc, 9-bolt flywheel
facts.note: Multiple vendors consistently list 240 mm for the 930 Turbo clutch. Patrick Motorsports sells OE-style billet flywheels at 240 mm with 9 bolt pattern.

facts.value: 135 teeth, internal diameter approximately 230 mm, external diameter approximately 280 mm
facts.note: One Design911 listing gives 225 mm internal diameter; another gives 230 mm. The 135 teeth count is consistent. The earlier 3.0 Turbo (1975-77) used a 130-tooth ring gear for the 12V starter.

facts.value: Clockwise as viewed from the pulley (rear/fan) end of the engine
facts.note: Multiple forum sources confirm clockwise rotation viewed from the rear. Pelican Parts and Rennlist posts agree. The distributor (driven at half speed) turns counterclockwise.

facts.value: Maximum permissible speed 6700 rpm; governor cutoff 7000 +/- 200 rpm; maximum constant speed 6000 rpm
facts.note: These figures are attributed to the 1976 930 workshop manual by a Pelican Parts poster. Forum consensus places the practical redline at 6700-6800 rpm. The tachometer has a marked red zone.

facts.value: 900 +/- 50 rpm (warm engine)
facts.note: Standard for warm-idle setting on K-Jetronic equipped 930 Turbo engines.

facts.item: Intermediate shaft position and center distance
facts.value: Below the crankshaft, center distance approximately 84 mm
facts.note: The 84 mm center distance comes from a third-party 911 SC engine model (secondary source, cited in the HANDOVER.md). The intermediate shaft runs at half engine speed. It is a long hollow shaft approximately the length of the crankshaft.

facts.item: Intermediate shaft gear and sprocket layout
facts.value: One 48-tooth aluminum timing gear (bolted on with lock tabs) driving off the 28-tooth crank gear; two 24-tooth chain sprockets (pressed on, held by snap rings) driving the cam chains
facts.note: The gear mesh (28/48) combined with the chain ratio (24/28) gives the required 1/2 speed reduction. The oil pump connects to the far end via a splined driveshaft held by a snap ring.

facts.value: Dry-sump gear-type oil pump with 4 stages (1 pressure stage + 3 scavenge stages); located at the bottom of the engine
facts.note: Naturally aspirated engines used 3-stage pumps; the turbo engines use a 4-stage pump. The scavenge housing on the 3.3 is cast iron. The pump is driven from the intermediate shaft at half engine speed via a splined driveshaft. Total oil capacity 13 liters.

facts.value: The pressure section is common to the 935, 930 3.3, 964 Turbo, 993 Turbo, GT3, GT3R and 996 Turbo; the differences lie in the scavenge sections
facts.note: This is a forum claim from an experienced builder. The 3.3 scavenge housing is cast iron while later versions are aluminum.

facts.value: 118 mm on all Porsche flat-six engines
facts.note: Confirmed by Porsche's own Christophorus magazine: 'one thing that all members of the boxer family have in common is their cylinder spacing: invariably 118 millimetres.'

facts.item: Bank stagger (cylinder offset between left and right banks)
facts.value: Approximately 59 mm (half the bore spacing), with the left bank (cylinders 1-2-3) sitting further forward toward the flywheel
facts.note: No web source confirms the exact offset in mm. The 59 mm figure (half of 118 mm bore spacing) is geometrically logical for a boxer with adjacent crankpins. A hobby software project cites 59 mm for the 993 flat-six. The handover document also uses this figure as [M]. Needs confirmation from a crankshaft drawing or top-view photo.

facts.item: Engine dry weight (with exhaust, intake, flywheel; without A/C)
facts.value: Approximately 419 lbs (190 kg)
facts.note: A Pelican Parts poster measured a 930/10 engine at 419 lbs dry with exhaust, intake, and flywheel but without A/C, and states this matches the Porsche 'Tech Book.' Another poster measured a 930/02 at the same weight. Wikipedia gives the flat-six family dry weight range as 176-230 kg.

facts.value: Roughly 700 mm flywheel face to pulley, 770 mm across valve covers, 600-650 mm tall with fan
facts.note: No web source gives engine-only envelope dimensions. These figures are from the HANDOVER.md as [M] estimates. All searches returned only whole-car dimensions. Needs measurement from a dimensioned factory drawing or a known-good 3D scan.

facts.item: Crank throw order from flywheel end
facts.value: Probably 1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6 (left bank cylinder first in each pair, moving from flywheel toward pulley)
facts.note: No web source gives the throw order explicitly. This follows from the firing order 1-6-2-4-3-5 with the left bank leading (closer to flywheel). The HANDOVER.md lists this as [M]. A crankshaft drawing or top-view photo is needed to confirm which bank leads.

facts.value: Screwed into the right side of the crankcase near the oil thermostat and crankcase breather cover, forming a triangle of three components
facts.note: Forum description places the oil pressure sender, oil thermostat, and crankcase breather cover near each other. The sender is the larger unit on a reducer fitting.

facts.value: 6.750 inches (171.5 mm) overall, M10 x 1.5 threads on both ends, ARP kit 204-4206
facts.note: This is an aftermarket ARP/Inconel 718 stud dimension, not the OEM Dilavar length. The OEM stud length was not found in any source. The ARP kit is listed as a direct replacement for the 1965-1998 air-cooled 911/930.

facts.value: 7.0:1 (factory specification)
facts.note: Consistently cited across all sources. One owner measured an actual CR of 6.58:1 with 90.6 cc chambers, suggesting factory specification and actual may differ. The 3.0 Turbo (1975-77) was 6.5:1.

conflicts: MAIN JOURNAL DIAMETER (60 mm vs 64 mm): The tech-racingcars wiki [S10] lists main bearing diameter as 60 mm (shown as '60-55 mm' for the 1978 engine). LN Engineering's journal diameter table [S20] lists 64 mm for all 2.7-3.3 L engines. Forum posts quoting the 964/930 shop manual give ~60 mm (59.97-59.99 mm). Earlier 2.0-2.4 L engines used 55 mm mains per LN or ~57 mm per forum sources. TRUST: The LN Engineering table is from a specialist vendor that manufactures Porsche engine bearings, so the 64 mm figure may be the housing bore (outer diameter of the bearing shell) rather than the crank journal diameter. The 60 mm figure likely refers to the crank journal itself. The factory workshop manual (WKD 481 321) is the definitive source; its page 46 was referenced but could not be read due to OCR issues.

ROD JOURNAL WIDTH (21.74 mm vs 21.8 mm vs 22 mm): Aftermarket rod vendors (Piratamotor, Hench) list 21.74 mm big-end width. Paul Frere's book gives 21.8 mm. Rennlist forum says '55 mm diameter x 22 mm wide.' These are very close and may reflect manufacturing tolerance vs nominal dimension. TRUST: Frere's book (21.8 mm) as a published reference, noting the vendor figure of 21.74 mm may be the actual aftermarket part width.

ROD LENGTH (127 mm vs 127.75 mm): The Mahle application guide PDF lists 127 mm for the 3.3 L Turbo. The tech-racingcars wiki gives 127.75 mm. Multiple aftermarket rod vendors list 127.75 mm. TRUST: 127.75 mm is probably the more precise OEM figure; 127 mm is a rounded number. Use 127.75 mm for modeling if confirmed by the workshop manual.

RING GEAR INTERNAL DIAMETER (225 mm vs 230 mm): One Design911 listing gives internal diameter 225 mm; another gives 230 mm. Both list external diameter 280 mm and 135 teeth. TRUST: Cannot determine which is correct without measuring or checking the Porsche parts catalog. The discrepancy may be between the pitch diameter and the actual inner bore.

BORE (97.0 mm vs 97.6 mm): The tech-racingcars wiki [S10] gives 97.6 mm bore for the 1978 car. Every other source (Stuttcars, Auto-Data, Wikipedia, Mahle) says 97.0 mm. The arithmetic check: pi/4 x 97.0^2 x 74.4 x 6 = 3298.8 cc matches the stated 3299 cc. TRUST: 97.0 mm is correct; 97.6 mm is an error on the wiki.

PISTON CROWN VOLUME (14.2 cc vs 38.5 cc in Mahle data): The Mahle PDF text extraction shows 14.2 cc for the 930 Turbo 3.3 L to 3.4 L piston (PS98-009), but also shows 38.5 cc in another column. The table layout in the extracted PDF text is garbled. TRUST: 14.2 cc is the most commonly cited figure in vendor listings for this kit. The 38.5 cc figure may belong to a different piston in the table (possibly the higher-compression 3.2 Carrera set).

facts.item: Stock 930 turbo camshaft duration at 1 mm lift
facts.value: Intake 214 degrees / Exhaust 202 degrees
facts.note: Dougherty Racing Cams profile table for 'Porsche 930 turbo' stock cam, 49 mm journal. These are the most widely cited figures in the 930 community.

facts.item: Stock 930 turbo camshaft duration at 0.050 inch lift
facts.value: Intake 208 degrees / Exhaust 197 degrees
facts.note: Same Dougherty Racing profile table.

facts.item: Stock 930 turbo cam lobe lift (at cam, before rocker ratio)
facts.value: Intake 0.368 inch (9.35 mm) / Exhaust 0.339 inch (8.61 mm)
facts.note: Zero lash, theoretical rocker ratio. Actual valve lift = lobe lift x rocker ratio.

facts.item: Stock 930 turbo cam lobe separation angle (LSA)
facts.value: 108 degrees
facts.note: Dougherty Racing table.

facts.item: Stock 930 turbo cam timing overlap-TDC lift setting
facts.value: 0.65 to 0.80 mm intake valve lift at TDC overlap (with 0.1 mm valve clearance)
facts.note: Dougherty lists 0.80 mm; forum sources say 0.65-0.80 mm range. This is the factory timing check value at TDC with 0.1 mm lash set.

facts.item: Stock 930 turbo cam event timing (forum-reported, 930/02 engine code)
facts.value: Intake opens 1 deg BTDC, closes 53 deg ABDC; Exhaust opens 43 deg BBDC, closes 3 deg ATDC
facts.note: Quoted from a published reference on Pelican Parts forum. Engine 930/02, not 930/60. The poster noted these figures do not fully reconcile with the duration and lobe-center values. Conflicts with other forum-reported numbers; treat as approximate.

facts.item: Alternate stock 930 cam event timing (forum-reported, citing Wayne Dempsey book for 1986 930)
facts.value: Intake opens 3 deg ATDC, closes 37 deg ABDC; Exhaust opens 27 deg BBDC, closes 5 deg BTDC
facts.note: Forum poster citing 'Wayne's book' for an 1986 930. These differ from the 930/02 figures, possibly reflecting a different measurement method or cam variant.

facts.item: SC cam on turbo duration at 1 mm lift
facts.value: Intake 236 degrees / Exhaust 224 degrees
facts.note: SC cam (also used in 911 SC 3.0 and Carrera 3.2) when fitted to a 930 turbo. Overlap TDC setting 1.4-1.7 mm.

facts.value: Approximately 1.4:1 average (up to ~1.5:1 at cam nose)
facts.note: Elgin Cams lists 1.4:1 average rocker arm ratio. Forum sources note ratio varies across the lobe profile, reaching ~1.5:1 at peak lift.

facts.value: 18 mm
facts.note: Parts listing gives bushing dimensions: shaft dia 18 mm, housing bore 20 mm, bushing width 26 mm. Fits 911 1965-1989.

facts.value: 12 rocker arms total (one per valve), each on its own individual rocker shaft, with 24 rocker shaft seals. Single cam per bank actuates both intake and exhaust rockers.
facts.note: Parts kit includes 12 rocker arms, 12 rocker shafts, 12 screws, 12 hex nuts, 24 shaft seals. Each rocker shaft is secured in the cam housing by tapered alloy plugs with a central M6 cap-head screw.

facts.value: 0.10 mm (0.004 inch) cold, both intake and exhaust
facts.note: Pelican Parts technical article for 911 and 914-6 engines 1965 onward. Same clearance for intake and exhaust.

facts.value: Intake approx 25-25.5 deg from cylinder axis, exhaust approx 30-30.25 deg; total included angle approx 55-56 degrees
facts.note: Forum measurements on 3.0/3.2 era heads (same family as 930 3.3). Hagerty article quotes 59 degrees total for the original Mezger design which may refer to earlier 2.0-2.7 heads. Values measured from the valve stem to the cylinder bore axis.

facts.value: Intake 49 mm head diameter, exhaust 41.5 mm head diameter; both with 9 mm stem diameter
facts.note: 930 Turbo 1978-89. Sodium-cooled exhaust valves.

facts.value: Intake 110.1 mm, exhaust 108.4 mm (diameter x stem x overall length: 49 x 9 x 110.1 mm intake, 41.5 x 9 x 108.4 mm exhaust)
facts.note: Design911 listing for 1978-89 930 Turbo valves.

facts.value: 45 degrees
facts.note: Listed for intake and exhaust valve sets.

facts.item: Number of valve springs per valve
facts.value: 2 (dual concentric springs with inner damper spring)
facts.note: AASCO 9 mm dual spring kit for 930. Aftermarket description confirms factory uses dual springs.
Forum poster quoting Porsche factory service manual specification, measured with Porsche special tool 9138/1.

facts.value: One separate cast-aluminum head per cylinder (6 individual heads per engine), each with cooling fins, intake port on upper (inboard) face, exhaust port on lower (outboard) face, single spark plug per cylinder
facts.note: Hagerty article on the air-cooled flat-six describes separate cylinders, SOHC, two valves per cylinder. Intake top / exhaust bottom orientation is standard for air-cooled 911; confirmed by forum observation that exhaust side runs hotter and is on the underside.

facts.value: Domed (hemispherical-type, though technically not a true hemisphere); commonly called 'hemi' but Hagerty article notes this is a misnomer
facts.note: Mezger designed domed combustion chambers with splayed valves. A true hemisphere would be too deep for good combustion.

facts.value: 32 mm
facts.note: Rennlist forum discussion. Common recommendation is to open to 36 mm for performance.

facts.value: M14 x 1.25 thread, 19 mm (3/4 inch) reach, 21 mm hex. OE type Bosch WR7DC or equivalent; 6 plugs per engine, one per cylinder
facts.note: Bosch WR7DC listed for 930 Turbo 1977-89 on Design911. Some sources list W3DP for earlier models. Heat range varies by market and model year.

facts.value: One per bank (2 total), spanning three cylinder heads. Four camshaft bearing journals per housing, 49 mm bore diameter (from 1976 onward on 930 turbo). Oil spray bar running through the housing. Housing bolts down over the three individual heads per bank.
facts.note: Forum discussion on cam tower bore sizes. 930 turbo engines from 1975/76 onward used 4-bearing, 49 mm bore housings. Earlier 47 mm housings exist but had oiling issues on the fourth journal.

facts.item: Oil spray bar in cam housing
facts.value: Central oil spray bar runs through the cam housing, feeds oil to cam journals and rocker arms. Orientation matters during installation.
facts.note: Early engines used center-oiled camshafts, later switched to spray bar because center oiling was inadequate at low RPM. Plugged at each end of housing.

facts.item: Oil return tubes between heads/cam housing and crankcase
facts.value: 4 per engine (2 per cylinder bank/head pair), telescopic/collapsible design
facts.note: MecaTechnic lists 4 per engine (2 per cylinder head). One-piece (OE) or two-piece (aftermarket for in-situ replacement) versions available. Part 93010704001 (two-piece) or 90110735101 (one-piece).

facts.value: Upper (intake side) and lower (exhaust side) per bank = 4 covers total. Cast magnesium (original) or aluminium (replacement). Upper cover secured by approximately 6 M8 nylock nuts with washers per cover. Covers have longitudinal ribbing for stiffness.
facts.note: FVD and LN Engineering describe replacing warped factory magnesium covers. Upper covers sold with 6 washers and 6 self-locking nuts per cover (2 covers per engine). Lower cover nut count not separately confirmed. 34 total nuts reported for a 993 (all 4 covers) on Rennlist; 930 count may differ.

facts.value: Duplex (double-row) roller chain, split type with master link. Chain size designation D67ZN, 98 links per chain. Two chains per engine (one per bank).
facts.note: Design911 listing for 911 1965-1989 and 964. Part 911-105-529-51 with master link 901-105-530-00. Same chain used across the air-cooled 911 range.
Standard for duplex D67ZN chains used on the 911 engine family. No web source found confirming this for the 930 specifically.

facts.value: 6 rails total per engine: 5 black plastic + 1 brown plastic. The brown rail sits on one of the lower positions (sources disagree whether lower-left or lower-right). Longer pointed end of each rail faces toward the nearest sprocket.
facts.note: Heritage Parts Centre lists black rail 91110522206 and brown rail 911.105.222.05. All six should be replaced together. Brown rail is slightly thicker, compensating for chain slack at that position.

facts.value: Mechanical (1965-1983), part 930-105-053-04; hydraulic sealed (from ~1984 on 930 3.3), part 930-105-058-03
facts.note: FVD lists mechanical tensioner for 911/930/914-6 1965-83. Hydraulic versions used from ~1984 on later 930 and 911 Carrera 3.2 models. One tensioner per bank (2 per engine).

facts.value: Single intermediate shaft running front-to-rear along the engine centerline, driven by a gear on the crankshaft (28-tooth crank gear meshing with 48-tooth IMS gear). IMS has one chain sprocket at each end (24 teeth each); front sprocket drives right bank (cyl 4-5-6) chain, rear sprocket drives left bank (cyl 1-2-3) chain. Cam sprockets have 28 teeth.
facts.note: Tooth counts from already-established data. The IMS chain drive path: crank gear -> IMS gear (at 1:1.714 ratio); IMS sprocket (24T) -> cam sprocket (28T). Crank turns 2x per 1x cam revolution. Each bank's chain runs at opposite ends of the IMS.

facts.value: Camshafts rotate in the same direction as the crankshaft: clockwise viewed from the pulley/fan end (-X end), counterclockwise viewed from the flywheel/gearbox end (+X end)
facts.note: No authoritative web source confirmed this. The chain drive (no idler gear between IMS sprocket and cam sprocket) means the cam sprocket rotates opposite the IMS sprocket, and the IMS gear rotates opposite the crank gear. Net result: cam same direction as crank. Forum posts describe cams turning counterclockwise 'while engine runs' but do not specify viewing direction.

facts.value: Clockwise viewed from the pulley/fan end (rear bumper side); counterclockwise viewed from the flywheel/gearbox end
facts.note: Rennlist forum confirms standard Porsche engine rotation. All Porsche flat-sixes rotate the same direction.

facts.value: One chain housing per bank (2 total), bolted to the crankcase at the pulley/fan end (-X end) of each bank. Roughly semi-circular covers enclosing the cam chain, sprockets, tensioner, and guide rails. Chain housing gaskets seal between housing and crankcase.
facts.note: Eurospares exploded diagram for 1977 911 Turbo chain case/camshaft housing. Chain housing also carries the chain tensioner mounting.

facts.value: Driven from the end of the left-bank (driver's side, cylinders 1-2-3) camshaft, via an air pump pulley arrangement with two allen-bolt heads engaging the pump shaft
facts.note: 930 turbo camshafts have a drive boss on the end for the scavenge pump. SC/NA cams lack this boss. The air pump pulley bolts drive the scavenge pump. Located at the sprocket end of the left-bank cam.

conflicts: Valve included angle: Hagerty article states 59 degrees total (attributed to Mezger's original design), but Pelican Parts forum measurements on 3.0/3.2 era heads (same family as 930 3.3) give approximately 55-56 degrees (25-25.5 intake + 30-30.25 exhaust). The 59 degree figure may apply to earlier 2.0-2.7 heads. The 3.0+ heads have a wider combustion chamber and larger valves, which one poster says explains the smaller included angle. I trust the forum measurements for the 3.0/3.2/3.3 head, but verify against a machinist's measurement.

Stock 930 cam event timing degrees: Multiple conflicting sets. (A) 930/02 reference: IO 1 BTDC, IC 53 ABDC, EO 43 BBDC, EC 3 ATDC. (B) Wayne Dempsey book for 1986 930: IO 3 ATDC, IC 37 ABDC, EO 27 BBDC, EC 5 BTDC. (C) 911 Performance Handbook: IO 7 BTDC, IC 47 ABDC, EO 49 BBDC, EC 3 BTDC. These cannot all be correct for the same cam. The discrepancy likely arises from different engine codes (930/02 vs 930/60 vs 930/66), different measurement points (seat-to-seat vs 1 mm lift vs 0.050 inch), or different valve clearance settings. The Dougherty duration figures (214/202 at 1 mm) are the most consistently cited and I trust those over any single set of open/close degrees.

Stock 930 cam overlap TDC lift setting: Dougherty Racing lists 0.80 mm, forum sources cite a range of 0.65-0.80 mm for stock 930 cams, while SC cams on turbo use 1.4-1.7 mm. The 0.65-0.80 mm range appears most reliable for the stock 930 turbo cam.

Distributor rotation direction: US-spec 930 uses CCW, Euro-spec uses CW. Some forum posts confuse the two. Permatune installation guide distinguishes them by ignition module pin count (6-pin = CCW/US, 8-pin = CW/Euro). I trust the Permatune document.

Stock 930 cam lobe lift: Dougherty lists 0.368/0.339 inch. One forum poster gives 0.378/0.343 inch. Another gives Group B at 0.374/0.339 inch. I trust the Dougherty figures as they maintain a consistent profile database.

Chain guide rail brown position: Sources disagree on whether the brown rail goes on the lower-left or lower-right side of the engine. Check a Porsche workshop manual or parts diagram for the correct position on your specific engine.

Whether the stock 1978-1985 turbo is called 3LDZ or K27: The 3LDZ designation comes from KKK's older naming system. Some sources treat the 3LDZ as a K27 family member, others as a K26 variant. The confusion arises because KKK rebranded and renumbered its product lines. For modelling purposes, the physical differences between variants (housing size, wheel dimensions) matter more than the naming.

facts.item: Intake air path sequence (930/60 K-Jetronic turbo)

facts.note: 90A unit part 911 603 120 05 (Bosch AL-401-X) for 1984-89. 70A unit AL9341X for earlier cars. The alternator is concentric within the cooling fan - removing the fan requires removing the alternator.

facts.value: Part 964 106 251 20 (also fits 911/914/930). Steel band with yellow zinc plating (stock finish) that secures the fan housing.
facts.note: Also available in titanium aftermarket version. The strap clamps around the fan housing to hold the two halves together.

facts.item: Engine oil cooler type and position
facts.value: Tubular (trombone/snake) type for 1974-1983 (OEM 930 207 050 03); radiator type for 1984-1989 (OEM 930 207 053 02/04). Mounted in right front fender/wheelhouse, in the blower air stream. 15 rows of tubes, 16 rows of fins (OEM spec per CSF).
facts.note: CSF replacement has 50 mm core vs OEM 45 mm. The workshop manual confirms: oil cooler mounted on engine block, in blower air stream; cooler coils in front right wheelhouse.

facts.value: Thermostatically controlled oil cooling. Oil thermostat sits on top of the engine next to the oil pressure switch. Oil pressure at 5500 rpm: approx. 4.0 bar at 80 deg C. Max oil temp: approx. 150 deg C.
facts.note: Workshop manual Technical Data page.

facts.value: On top of the engine near the crankcase breather cover, at the bulkhead side. The turbo oil feed comes off the same location as the low oil pressure switch.
facts.note: Forum description. Oil temperature sender is on the right chain housing, vertical portion.

facts.item: Turbo oil feed and scavenge system
facts.value: Oil feed from a banjo fitting near the oil pressure switch, with a restrictor ball under the banjo bolt to limit flow. Scavenge pump returns oil from the turbo's oil drip tank. The scavenge tank's breather tube runs up through the engine tray to a hose to the air cleaner box.
facts.note: Composite from Rennlist threads. Factory scavenge pump only falls behind incoming oil below 1500 RPM at idle.

facts.value: Oil filler neck on top of the crankcase. Crankcase breather cover on top of engine at bulkhead side. Oil tank is in the car body (right rear fender area), not on the engine.
facts.note: Oil system: dry sump, 13 litres total capacity. The oil tank is not part of the engine assembly.

facts.value: Transformer-type CDI (capacitive discharge ignition), breakerless, Bosch. Called 'CD!' in workshop manual (OCR error for CDI). 6-pin CDI module used 1978-1989 on the turbo.
facts.note: Workshop manual Technical Data page confirms CDI. Perma-Tune says 6-pin module 1978-1989 on turbo. European 930 uses 8-pin connectors with clockwise distributor per Perma-Tune.

facts.value: Counterclockwise (US-spec 930 turbo). European spec uses clockwise rotation with 8-pin CDI connectors.
facts.note: Conflict: Perma-Tune says US=CCW, Euro=CW. Forum posts confirm CCW for most 930 turbos. A 5K ohm resistor in the coil wire is required with 6-pin CDI to prevent damage.

facts.value: At the left rear of the engine, driven from a gear on the crank nose at half crank speed
facts.note: Standard air-cooled 911 architecture. The distributor gear meshes with a gear on the crankshaft or intermediate shaft at the pulley end.
Stoddard parts listing. Cap and rotor shared between 911 SC and 930 Turbo.

facts.value: Bosch W3DPO (factory fitment for 930 turbo). Gap 0.6 mm (0.024 in). NGK equivalent: BP8EVX (also BP8ES).
facts.note: Forum consensus. W3DPO is very cold. Some owners run one step warmer (W4CS). The W5DPO is listed for 1975-77 911 Turbo (3.0L). Thread size 14 mm, reach 19 mm per Denso cross-reference.

facts.item: Spark plug access and lead routing
facts.value: Spark plugs on the upper side of each head, accessed through openings in the engine shroud/tin. Plug leads route along each bank from the distributor at the left rear.
facts.note: Standard air-cooled 911 architecture. The spark plug sits between intake and exhaust ports on each head.

facts.value: Beru steel-encased ignition lead harness, part 911 609 010 07, set of six leads plus coil lead. Fits 930 Turbo 1975-1989. Color: black.
facts.note: Design911 listing says 'HT lead set comes in black'. No factory source confirms red or blue leads for the 930 Turbo.

facts.value: Early cars: mounted on the fan housing. Later cars: mounted on the left-side electrical panel in the engine bay. Coil is Bosch type (or Marelli BAE202B on some years).
facts.note: Forum post from SC owner describing coil moved from fan housing to left-side panel on later models. CDI box is in the rear engine compartment near the fuses.

facts.value: 29 deg BTDC +/-2 deg at 4000 rpm (manual page 157). At idle 1000+/-50 rpm: approximately 0-2 deg. Advance curve is centrifugal, plotted against distributor shaft speed.
facts.note: USA spec: 5 deg ATDC +/-3 deg at 950+/-50 rpm. Page 165 gives 31 deg +/-4 deg BTDC at 4000 rpm for Europe/California/Japan.

facts.value: All 930 engines fitted with an air pump to reduce exhaust emissions regardless of destination. US-market 49-state cars (930/61) had thermal reactors. California cars (930/63) had vacuum control. Belt for air injection pump fits 930 Turbo 1978-1989.
facts.note: Supercar Nostalgia says all 930s had air pump. Rennlist forum contradicts, saying European cars had no air pump. The workshop manual notes to take care not to damage the secondary air injection pipes during engine removal.

facts.value: York upright compressor (1978-1979 930 turbo stock). Nippondenso compressor appeared on later cars (from roughly VIN 1000). York operates vertically on 78-79 3.3 930. A/C belt: 13 x 1200 mm (Nippondenso). Belt-driven from the crankshaft.
facts.note: European-market 1978-83 930 turbo: A/C was optional. The compressor is belt-driven on the right side of the engine. No air injection pump on European spec per some forum sources (contradicted by Supercar Nostalgia).

facts.value: Fan/alternator V-belt (always). A/C compressor belt (if equipped, optional). Air injection pump belt (disputed: some sources say all markets, some say US only).
facts.note: No power steering pump on the 930 until late models. European cars are simpler; US cars have more emissions equipment.

facts.value: Engine carrier support cross member bracket: 930 375 011 01. Fabricated steel. Mounts engine/transmission to the chassis at rear. Engine carrier bolts torque: 9.0 mkg (65 ft-lb).
facts.note: Workshop manual confirms 9.0 mkg for engine carrier hex head screws. Patrick Motorsports also sells an RSR aluminium replacement. Attached with M12 bolts.

facts.value: Rear engine support bracket: 930 115 014 00, fits 930 Turbo 1978-1989. Bolts the engine to the crossbar.
facts.note: Stoddard lists this as fitting 1978-1989 911 and 911 Turbo.

facts.value: Part 911 375 043 00 (also 911 375 043 02/03). Rubber transmission/engine mount. Used on all 911/912/930 from 1965-1989.
facts.note: Stoddard parts listing. This rubber mount sits between the engine bracket and the crossbar.

facts.value: 8-piece aluminium baffle kit, parts include 930 106 228 00 (x6), 930 106 023 01 (x4), 930 106 221 01 (x2), 930 106 222 01 (x2). Plus cylinder air baffle kit 930 106 220K. These sit under and around the cylinders to direct cooling air.
facts.note: OE Match replacement kit. OEM was mild steel; aftermarket upgrades use stainless steel. The tin directs cooling air from the fan shroud down over and under the finned cylinders and heads.

facts.value: Cast magnesium alloy (Elektron), natural/bare finish with machined mating surfaces. Aluminium alloy on some later variants.
facts.note: Standard air-cooled 911 architecture. The case halves are typically unfinished magnesium/aluminium alloy, grey in appearance.

facts.value: Cast aluminium or magnesium fan. Factory finish is bare/natural metal (silver/grey). Fan center, pulley and housing strap have yellow zinc plating as stock finish.
facts.note: Forum poster says fan center, pulley and housing strap are plated in yellow zinc as stock finish. The fan blades themselves are typically bare aluminium.

facts.value: Aluminium (not magnesium like pre-1978). Upper valve covers are unpainted aluminium. They expand at the same rate as cam towers, reducing warpage. Black wrinkle paint is an aftermarket/later finish.
facts.note: Pelican Parts article. Pre-1978 covers were magnesium. The turbo aluminium covers look similar but differ in thermal expansion. Some owners paint them in black wrinkle or powder coat.

facts.value: Air-to-air intercooler, lies flat under the rear spoiler (tea tray). The spoiler was raised and enlarged for 1978 to accommodate it. Visible from above/rear when engine lid is open.
facts.note: Intercooler reduced intake temperature from ~140-150 deg C to ~50-60 deg C in testing.

facts.value: Factory vacuum and coolant hoses: black rubber. Silicone replacement hose kits available in various colors.
facts.note: DO88 replacement hose kit for K-Jetronic. OEM hoses are black rubber that becomes brittle with age.

facts.value: Firing order 1-6-2-4-3-5. Left bank (car's left, +Y) cylinders 1-2-3, right bank (-Y) cylinders 4-5-6. No. 1 nearest flywheel, No. 6 furthest (pulley end).
facts.note: Workshop manual confirms firing order. Cylinder numbering is standard Porsche convention.

facts.value: Approximately 700 mm flywheel to pulley (X axis), approximately 770 mm across valve covers (Y axis), approximately 600-650 mm tall with fan (Z axis above crank). With intercooler and exhaust, taller.
facts.note: From the HANDOVER.md document section 8. These are sanity-check estimates, not measured values.

facts.value: 9.0 mkg (65 ft-lb) for engine and transmission carrier hex head screws
facts.note: Workshop manual page 32 (installation notes). Drive shaft flange capscrews: 8.3 mkg (60 ft-lb).

facts.value: Control pressure warm: 6.0-6.7 bar (test), 6.2-6.5 bar (adjusting). Cold: temperature-dependent, approximately 2.9-3.65 bar. Injector opening pressure: 2.1 +/-0.1 bar. Control circuit delivery rate: 160-240 cm3/min.
facts.note: Workshop manual page 113 test/adjusting values. OCR somewhat garbled; verify against scanned page.

facts.value: Both pumps together: at least 1170 cm3/30 sec
facts.note: Two fuel pumps: one near the fuel tank at front, one at rear near gearbox/engine.

facts.value: Fabricated steel cross member, spans the rear of the engine bay. Inner and outer parts available separately (DANSK). The crossbar bolts to the body at both ends and the engine/transmission mounts to it via rubber mounts and brackets.
facts.note: No dimensions found. Some cars have aluminium replacement cross members which require additional mounting brackets (911 341 031 01). Patrick Motorsports sells an RSR-style steel replacement.

facts.item: US vs Euro engine differences summary
facts.value: Euro 930/60: 300 PS, K-Jetronic, red shroud. US 930/61 (49-state): 265 HP, thermal reactors, different emissions equipment. US 930/63 (California): 265 HP, vacuum control. 1986+ US 930/68: 282 HP, LE-Jetronic with DME, Lambda sensors, 3-way catalytic converter.
facts.note: 1986 US cars switched from K-Jetronic to LE-Jetronic with DME engine management. The European model kept K-Jetronic until end of production.

facts.item: 930 Turbo engine type codes by year
facts.note: Workshop manual general specifications page. The 930/66 is essentially the same engine with minor updates (new warm-up regulator 1983, revised chain tensioners 1984).

conflicts: Distributor rotation: Perma-Tune says US-spec 930 is counterclockwise, Euro-spec is clockwise (8-pin). Multiple forum posts say the 930 turbo distributor is counterclockwise. The Bentley manual also states counterclockwise for the 911 family. Trust the CCW direction for most 930 turbos; the Euro clockwise claim from Perma-Tune may refer to a specific aftermarket replacement.

Air injection pump: Supercar Nostalgia says all 930 engines had an air pump regardless of destination. Rennlist forum posts say European cars had no air pump system. The workshop manual mentions secondary air injection pipes, suggesting the pump exists on the car being documented. Trust the reference site (Supercar Nostalgia) over forum claims, but verify against a European-spec parts catalog.

Fan belt dimensions: Sources disagree between 9.5x710, 10x710, 10x713, and 9.5x725 mm. The 710 mm length appears to be stock for 1.67:1 ratio; 725 mm is for the upgraded 1.8:1 ratio with different pulleys. Heritage Parts Centre lists 10x713 mm for 930 Turbo 1978-1989. Trust Heritage Parts for the production belt.

Fan shroud color: No factory documentation found. FVD sells a red GRP reproduction for the 930 Turbo. Forum posts mention red for S and Turbo models, green for E models, but these are anecdotal. Without factory confirmation, red is the best available answer for the 930 Turbo.

Intake manifold material: One vendor listing says magnesium, others imply aluminium. The 930 Turbo manifold (part 930 110 034 02) may be either depending on production date. No factory specification found.

Alternator rating by year: 70A for 1975-1977, but the 1978-1983 turbo rating is unclear -- could be 70A or 90A. 90A is confirmed only for 1984-1989. Some aftermarket listings suggest all 1978+ 930 turbos used 90A.
